integrationGuide.heading: Setup help
integrationGuide.intro: Step-by-step instructions for each token. Open one to see what it is for, where to get it, which permissions to grant and how to check that it works.
integrationGuide.save: Paste the token into the "{{field}}" field above and click "{{save}}". The field empties and the badge changes to "{{configured}}". To replace a token, paste the new one and save again; an empty field keeps the current token.
integrationGuide.test: There is no test button: a token is checked when a reference is fetched. Go to {{company}} → {{design}}, click "{{add}}", choose the type "{{kind}}" and paste the link. Reload the page after a moment: "{{ready}}" with a summary means the token works; "{{failed}}" shows the reason under the reference. After fixing the problem, click "{{refresh}}" on that reference.
integrationGuide.failMissing: No token has been saved yet. Save one above, then click "{{refresh}}" on the reference.
integrationGuide.failBadLink: The link is not in a supported form. Copy it again from the browser's address bar (see the link format above).
integrationGuide.failRateLimited: The provider is limiting requests. Wait a few minutes, then click "{{refresh}}".
integrationGuide.storage: Where it is kept: in AWS Secrets Manager (the voc/design-integrations secret, encrypted with the platform's KMS key). Only the settings API can read it, it is never shown again, and this page only reports whether a token is configured. To stop a token working at once, revoke it at the provider.
integrationGuide.otherCredentials: Data source credentials, such as the GitHub Issues token, are not set here: each source card in the {{plugins}} tab has its own fields and setup steps.

figma.title: Figma personal access token
figma.summary: Required to use Figma files as design references.
figma.purpose: Lets the platform read the Figma files you add as design references under {{company}} → {{design}}: page and frame names and published styles. The token is sent only to api.figma.com, and only when a Figma reference is fetched.
figma.step1: Sign in to Figma. In the file browser, open the account menu in the top-left corner and choose "Settings".
figma.step2: Open the "Security" tab. Under "Personal access tokens", click "Generate new token".
figma.step3: Give the token a name (for example "VoC design system") and choose an expiration.
figma.step4: In the scopes, set "File content" to read-only (file_content:read). Leave every other scope off.
figma.step5: Click "Generate token" and copy it straight away: Figma shows it only once.
figma.permissions: One scope only: file_content:read (read-only). A token can only see files its owner can open in Figma, so the account that creates it must have access to the files you reference.
figma.linkFormat: Figma link: https://www.figma.com/design/<file key>/… (/file/, /proto/ and /board/ links also work).
figma.failRefused: The token is wrong, expired or revoked, or it lacks file_content:read. Generate a new one and save it.
figma.failNotFound: The link is wrong, or the token's owner cannot open that file in Figma.
figma.security: The token acts as the Figma user who created it. Prefer an account that can only view the design files, set an expiration and save a replacement before it expires. If a token leaks, revoke it in Figma under Settings → Security; revocation is immediate.

github.title: GitHub fine-grained personal access token
github.summary: Optional for public repositories, required for private ones.
github.purpose: Lets the platform read design tokens, CSS, Tailwind configuration and README files from the GitHub repositories you add as design references under {{company}} → {{design}}. Public repositories also work without a token, at GitHub's lower anonymous rate limit; private repositories need one. The token is sent only to api.github.com.
github.step1: On GitHub, click your profile picture (top right) → "Settings" → "Developer settings" → "Personal access tokens" → "Fine-grained tokens", then "Generate new token". The link below opens the form already filled in.
github.step2: Enter a name and an expiration. Under "Resource owner", choose the user or organization that owns the design repository.
github.step3: Under "Repository access", choose "Only select repositories" and select only the design repositories.
github.step4: Under "Permissions", in the repository permissions, set "Contents" to "Read-only". "Metadata" (read-only) is added automatically. Grant nothing else.
github.step5: Click "Generate token" and copy it. If the organization requires approval, the token can only read public repositories until an organization owner approves it.
github.newToken: Create the token on GitHub (pre-filled: Contents read-only)
github.permissions: Contents: read-only, plus the automatic Metadata: read-only, on the selected repositories only. Avoid a classic token: it reaches every repository your account can access.
github.linkFormat: GitHub link: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>, a folder (…/tree/<branch>/<folder>) or a single file (…/blob/<branch>/<file>).
github.failRefused: The token is wrong, expired or revoked, or it lacks Contents read access.
github.failNotFound: The link is wrong, or the repository is private and the token was not given access to it (GitHub answers "not found" rather than "forbidden").
github.failNoFiles: The token works, but that location has no design files. Link the folder that holds them.
github.security: The token acts as the GitHub user who created it and stops working if that user loses access. Keep it limited to the design repositories, set an expiration and save a replacement before it expires. If it leaks, delete it under Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens. It is separate from the GitHub Issues data source token: do not reuse one for the other.
